desc:
You have n distinct item kinds numbered 0..n-1. Kind i can be used at most limits[i] times in total over all groups.

You want to form as many groups as possible. Every group must contain distinct kinds (no kind twice inside one group) and be non-empty, and when the groups are listed in order, each group must contain strictly more kinds than the group before it. Return the maximum possible number of groups.

limits = [1, 2, 5] -> 3   ({2}, {1,2}, {0,1,2})
limits = [2, 1, 2] -> 2
limits = [1, 1]    -> 1
hints: If you want k groups, the cheapest choice is group sizes 1, 2, ..., k, so you need k(k+1)/2 item uses in total and at least k distinct kinds.
A single kind can be used only once per group, but kinds with small limits are used up quickly. Think about adding kinds in increasing order of their limits and keeping the total supply seen so far.

Sort the limits. Walk through them in increasing order with a running total. Each time the total reaches (groups + 1)(groups + 2) / 2, one more group becomes affordable: increase the group count by one.
editorial: First, if k groups are possible then groups of sizes exactly 1, 2, ..., k are possible too (shrink the groups from the largest down; this only frees supply and keeps sizes strictly increasing). So we ask for the largest k such that groups of sizes 1..k can be filled. They need k(k+1)/2 uses in total, so the total supply must be at least that, and also at least k kinds are required.

Algorithm: sort the limits ascending, keep total (the sum of all limits seen so far) and groups (initially 0). For each limit add it to total; if total ≥ (groups + 1)(groups + 2) / 2 then the next group, of size groups + 1, can be afforded, so increase groups. Each kind can raise the count by at most one, which guarantees there are always enough distinct kinds: when groups reaches g, at least g kinds have been looked at.

Why the unused supply of small kinds can simply be carried forward: groups are built from the biggest down, so the biggest groups take one item from each of the kinds with the largest limits, while the leftover of the small-limit kinds is exactly what the small groups consume. A formal proof is a Hall-type counting argument; the randomized brute force (all ways to choose the groups) used for this problem confirms the rule. Sorting dominates: O(n log n).
